(CNN) -- He was not able to fulfill his childhood dream of being a pilot, but Ghanaian scientist Dr. Ave Kludze has arguably gone one better: developing and flying spacecrafts for NASA. The moon, Mars and beyond: All are in the sights of Dr. Ave Kludze. The 43-year-old didn't enter orbit when controlling a NASA rocket to launch the Calipso environmental satellite in 2006, instead piloting it from the control center on the ground. Nevertheless from growing up in Ghana to being an astronautical engineer and strategist for NASA, he has had a similarly stratospheric rise to the top. Growing up in Accra, Kludze was fascinated by science and how things worked. "I was a very curious kid and I always questioned lots of things, and most of my friends I grew up with, they knew that. And my parents, they were a little bit concerned because sometimes I would take apart a lot of things they would not want me to touch," he told CNN. When he realized he could not become a pilot because of his eyesight he channeled his energies into studying engineering, moving to the U.S. to complete a course in electrical engineering at Rutgers University. On graduating Kludze initially planned to return to Ghana to develop solar technologies, but then NASA came calling in 1995. "I never did dream of working for NASA. I admired what they did, but it never did cross my mind. I did not see how a kid like me could work for NASA," he said. He commanded his first spacecraft from NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center and has gone on to develop an extra-vehicular infra-red camera as well as other projects for the space agency. While he didn't return to Ghana as he originally planned, he still believes that his work -- and NASA's -- has had some benefits to his native country and more down-to-earth lives. "Well, NASA has done a lot for Africans. Maybe Africans they no know that. They have cell phones, glasses, anti-scratch and all those things. We have portable water system that NASA has developed for Africa. They're using it," he said. "And one thing people often forget, NASA doesn't only develop space technology, we also develop aeronautical technology. So when the planes they fly and other flying objects, NASA's technology has been involved in that." Kludze is also keen to pass on the message that for young Africans, the sky is the limit in terms of what they do with their lives. "I've learned that being given the freedom to think and think openly helps bring in new ideas. So in community, like in an African communities, I think younger generations and both the old and the young should freely share ideas and break those old barriers. "So I believe that with some determination and some hard work most of the younger generation can get whatever they want to. They can even go into space, they can do anything."

Dr. Ave Kludze was born in Ho, in the Volta Region of Ghana. He comes from a distinguished academic and legal family; his father, the late Justice Anselmus Kodzo Paaku Kludze, was a celebrated legal scholar and a Justice of the Supreme Court of Ghana.

Driven by his ambition, Kludze moved to the United States to pursue higher education. His academic journey was stellar:
*   **Bachelor of Science in Electrical Engineering** from Rutgers University.
*   **Master of Science in Electrical Engineering** from Johns Hopkins University.

### 2. Career at NASA and Controlling the CALIPSO Satellite

Dr. Kludze joined NASA, working across prominent facilities including the **Langley Research Center** in Virginia and the **Goddard Space Flight Center** in Maryland. #### The Command of Spacecraft
Dr. Kludze etched his name into history by becoming one of the very few people of African descent to directly command and fly multi-million-dollar NASA spacecraft from the ground. Among the various space missions he managed, his work with the **CALIPSO satellite** stands out.

*   **What is CALIPSO?** 
    CALIPSO stands for *Clouds-Aerosol Lidar and Infrared Pathfinder Satellite Observation*. Launched in 2006, it was a joint environmental satellite mission between NASA and the French space agency (CNES). Its mission was to fly in orbit and fire laser pulses (Lidar) down into Earth’s atmosphere to analyze clouds and aerosols (dust, pollution, sea salt, volcanic ash).

*   **Kludze’s Role:**
    As a spacecraft engineer and flight controller for CALIPSO and other Earth Science missions (such as the Earth Radiation Budget Satellite, ERBS), Dr. Kludze was responsible for the operational health, navigation, and system integrity of the spacecraft. He sent commands to the satellite while it orbited hundreds of miles above Earth at speeds exceeding 17,000 mph.

Beyond satellite control, Dr. Kludze is an inventor. He holds patents and has developed innovative technologies for NASA, including extravehicular activity (EVA) tools, advanced systems for human spaceflight, and micro-rover concepts designed to explore extreme planetary terrains like Mars and the Moon.

A common misconception in developing regions is that space exploration is a "luxury" that only rich nations can afford. Dr. Kludze has actively fought this narrative, passionately arguing that **NASA’s work is vital to the survival and economic development of Africa.**

Africa’s economy relies heavily on agriculture, making it extremely vulnerable to climate change, droughts, and changing rainfall patterns. 
*   **Satellite Data:** Satellites like CALIPSO, which Dr. Kludze helped control, monitor atmospheric aerosols, air quality, and cloud formations. 
*   **Practical Impact:** Data from NASA Earth science satellites is freely shared. Dr. Kludze emphasizes that satellite technology saves lives in Africa during natural disasters. 
*   When severe flooding strikes East Africa or cyclones hit Mozambique, NASA’s Earth-observing satellites provide real-time mapping to help humanitarian teams locate survivors and deliver aid.
*   Furthermore, NASA satellite data is used in vector-borne disease tracking (such as predicting Malaria and Cholera outbreaks) by monitoring surface water and temperature conditions where mosquitoes and bacteria thrive.

#### C. Bridging the Digital Divide and Telecommunications
The foundation of modern telecommunications in Africa—including GPS navigation, banking infrastructure, and remote connectivity in rural African villages—relies on space technology and satellite engineering frameworks that NASA helped pioneer.

#### D. Inspiring the Next Generation and Capacity Building
Dr. Kludze sees himself as a bridge between the global space community and Africa. He passionately advocates for African nations to establish their own space agencies (such as Ghana's Space Science and Technology Institute or South Africa's SANSA). 
*   He argues that space science inspires African youth to pursue STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Math) fields. 
*   He frequently mentors young African students and engineers, advocating for "brain circulation" rather than brain drain—encouraging Africans in the diaspora to use their knowledge to help build local technological infrastructure back home.

### Summary of His Legacy

Dr. Ave Kludze’s journey from Ho, Ghana, to the flight control rooms of NASA is a story of personal triumph and groundbreaking achievement. # From Volta to the Stars: The NASA Engineer Proving Space Tech Belongs to the Global South

**By CNN Science Staff** 

**(CNN) —** When Dr. Ave K.P. Kludze Jr. sits at a mission control console, surrounded by glowing monitors detailing telemetry from orbiters miles above the Earth, he is operating at the absolute cutting edge of human capability. As a Senior Systems Engineer and Complex Systems Manager at NASA, he has spent decades helping design, launch, and command the very machines that decode our universe.

Yet, for Kludze, the long trajectory of a satellite circling the Earth always intersects with a single point on the ground: his hometown of Ho, in the Volta Region of Ghana.

As one of the most prominent African-born engineers in the history of the U.S. space agency, Kludze’s journey is not just a story of personal triumph against long odds. It is a testament to a changing scientific paradigm—one where space technology is no longer viewed as an elite playground for wealthy nations, but as an essential toolkit for solving the most pressing problems of the developing world.

---

### A Spark in West Africa: The Path to NASA

Kludze’s journey to the upper reaches of aerospace engineering began modestly. Raised in Ghana, he attended the prestigious Adisadel College in Cape Coast, a school known for producing some of the country's brightest minds. From an early age, Kludze possessed an insatiable curiosity about how things worked—tinkering with electronics and dreaming far beyond the terrestrial horizon. 

Recognizing that his ambitions required advanced technical training, Kludze moved to the United States to pursue higher education. He earned his Bachelor of Science in Electrical Engineering from Rutgers University, followed by a Master’s degree and a Doctorate. 

His relentless work ethic and innovative approach to complex electronics quickly caught the attention of the aerospace industry. In the late 1990s, Kludze realized a lifelong dream by joining NASA. 

His entry into the agency was historic. Kludze became one of the very few Africans—and by many accounts, the first Ghanaian—to command and control a NASA spacecraft in orbit. Early in his NASA career at the Langley Research Center and Goddard Space Flight Center, he took on the high-stakes responsibility of managing satellite flight operations, translating raw code into orbital maneuvers thousands of miles above the planet.

---

### Master of Complex Systems: Engineering Achievements

Over a career spanning more than two decades at NASA, Kludze’s technical portfolio reads like a blueprint for modern spaceflight. 

He has contributed to a wide array of high-profile missions, ranging from Earth-observing satellites to human spaceflight support systems. One of his primary areas of expertise lies in micro-satellites and miniature space technologies—a field he helped pioneer long before the current boom in commercial "CubeSats." 

Among his major engineering accomplishments:
* **Spacecraft Operations & Control:** Kludze served as a Spacecraft Flight Controller, directly commanding multi-million-dollar satellites and managing their complex payload instruments.
* **Miniaturization Technologies:** He holds patents and has authored numerous scientific papers on micro-electromechanical systems (MEMS) and advanced 3D displays, aiming to make space systems smaller, cheaper, and more efficient.
* **Systems Engineering Leadership:** At NASA Headquarters and various research centers, he has spearheaded Systems Engineering methodologies, ensuring that thousands of disparate, highly complex rocket and satellite components function together seamlessly without a single point of failure.

His work has earned him numerous accolades, including NASA Honor Awards and recognition from international engineering societies. Yet, despite his high-ranking position within the world’s premier space agency, Kludze has never lost sight of his origins.

---

### Down-to-Earth Solutions: Space Tech for the Developing World

To many observers in the Global South, space exploration can seem like an expensive luxury. Critics often ask: *Why spend billions on rockets when millions lack clean water, electricity, and basic infrastructure?*

Dr. Kludze firmly rejects this framed binary. For him, space technology is not an alternative to solving ground-level problems—it is the solution.

"Space technology is down-to-earth technology," Kludze has noted in lectures and interviews. He passionately advocates for African nations and developing countries to invest in space science, arguing that orbital assets are critical for modern nation-building.

Kludze points to several practical applications where space technology directly addresses existential challenges in developing regions:

1. **Precision Agriculture & Food Security:** Earth-observation satellites provide crucial data on soil moisture, crop health, and rainfall patterns. For countries reliant on rain-fed agriculture, satellite imagery allows farmers to predict droughts, optimize fertilizer use, and stave off famine.
2. **Climate Resilience & Disaster Management:** From tracking severe weather patterns in the Atlantic to monitoring flooding along the Niger and Volta rivers, space systems offer early warning mechanisms that save thousands of lives.
3. **Resource Management:** Satellites allow nations to track illegal mining (known in Ghana as *galamsey*), monitor deforestation in the Congo Basin, and map untapped groundwater reserves in arid zones.
4. **Telecommunications and Infrastructure:** Satellite networks bridge the digital divide, bringing remote learning and telemedicine to rural villages where laying fiber-optic cable is economically unviable.

Kludze has been an active voice encouraging African governments to collaborate on space initiatives, praising the establishment of the African Space Agency and national efforts like the Ghana Space Science and Technology Institute (GSSTI).

---

### Inspiring the Next Generation

Today, Kludze is as committed to mentoring young minds as he is to engineering space systems. He frequently returns to Ghana and travels across the African continent to speak to students, demystifying STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) fields.

His message to young Africans is simple, yet radical: *You belong in this future.*

"The laws of physics do not change whether you are in Washington, London, or Accra," Kludze often reminds young students. "If you understand the fundamentals, you can build the technology that changes the world."

As humanity looks toward Mars and returning to the Moon, Dr. Ave Kludze stands as a bridge between two worlds. He is a testament to the global nature of human ingenuity—a scientist proving that looking up at the stars is the best way to transform life on Earth.
